short: He split his own party to repeal the Corn Laws, and founded the modern police.
full:
Robert Peel led two governments, briefly in 1834-35 and substantially from 1841 to 1846. As home secretary he had already created the Metropolitan Police in 1829, whose officers are still called bobbies. His Tamworth Manifesto of 1834 accepted the Reform Act and recast the Tories as a Conservative party willing to reform in order to preserve.

In office he restored the income tax in 1842 to fund sweeping tariff cuts, and passed the Bank Charter Act of 1844 fixing the Bank of England's monopoly on note issue. The Irish potato blight of 1845 convinced him that the Corn Laws, which kept grain prices high for landowners, had to go. He carried repeal in June 1846 with Whig votes and against two-thirds of his own party, and his government fell the same night on an Irish coercion bill. The split lasted a generation; the Peelites, Gladstone among them, eventually joined the Liberals.
